Before the Commissioner of Income-tax Appeals, NFAC 
In the matter of Raju 
Assessment Year: 2017-18 
Appeal No.: CIT (A), Delhi- 10/10047/2020-21 
Date of Hearing: 08.09.2021 
 
WRITTEN SUBMISSIONS ON VARIOUS GROUNDS OF APPEAL 
 
Ground No. 1 
(a)Re: That the learned Income Tax Officer has grossly erred both in 
law and on fact in completing the assessment under section 144 of the 
Act by computing the total income of Rs. 21,49,130/- and, thereby 
raising a demand of Rs. 1,07,59,591/-. 
 
(b) That in this connection, the learned Assessing Officer has erred in 
computing demand of Rs. 1,07,59,591/- on a total income of Rs. 
85,97,720/- (as per computation sheet) as against assessed total income 
of Rs. 21,49,130/- determined in the assessment order. 
 
 
1.1 The appellant is an individual who was engaged in the business of trading in grocery items. 
For the relevant assessment year, the learned assessing officer has completed the assessment 
under section 144 of Act vide order dated 07.12.2019 wherein the learned Assessing Officer 
has assessed the total income at Rs. 21,49,130/- and accordingly, raised a demand of Rs. 
1,07,59,591/-. On perusal of the assessment order, it had been noticed that the learned 
Assessing Officer had inadvertently computed the total income at Rs. 85,97,720/-(as per 
computation sheet) as assessed total income of Rs.21,49,130/- determined in the assessment 
order and accordingly raised the demand of Rs. 1,07,59,591/-.  
 
1.2 In this regard, the appellant had filed the rectification application dated 20th June, 2020. The 
learned assessing officer vide order no. ITBA/REC/S/154_1/2021- 22/1032302178(1) dated 8th 
April, 2021 rectified the mistake being apparent from record, wherein the learned Assessing 
Officer rectified the total Income from Rs. 85,97,720/- to Rs. 21,49,130/- and accordingly, the 
tax liability of the appellant had reduced from Rs. 1,07,59,591/- to Rs. 26,89,881/-. The 
rectification order is attached herewith as Annexure_1. 

 
1.3 Hence the ground-1 has been not been pressed in the written submission.  
 
Ground No.2 
(a)That the learned Assessing Officer has erred in completing the 
assessment under section 144 of the Act without the notice being 
served on the appellant, being a mandatory requirement under 
section 144 of the Act.  
 
 
 
(b)Than in this connection, the learned Assessing Officer has not 
given proper opportunity of being heard to the appellant and 
straight away passed the assessment order, thereby, violating the 
principles of natural justice. 
 
2.1 The appellant is running a small local grocery shop. The case of the appellant for the year 
under consideration, was selected for scrutiny and notice under section 142(1) of the Act was 
issued on 12.03.2018. As per the learned Assessing Officer, the said notice was duly served. 
However, the appellant did not receive the said notice. 
 
2.2 Thereafter, as per the assessment order, notice dated 18.09.2019 and 21.11.2019 was issued 
to the appellant. The learned assessing officer stated that “Thereafter, notice under section 
142(1) dated 18.09.2019 have been issued to the assessee and also got served upon the 
assessee through ITBA, Speed Post No. ED042632034IN, which is also remained uncompiled 
with”.  However, none of the notices were received by the appellant. It is pertinent to mention 
here that the appellant had not received the aforesaid notice. Copy of the screenshot of India 
post which shows the tracking of post using no. ED042632034IN is enclosed as Annexure_2.  
 
2.3 It is further submitted that no notice was even received by the appellant. However, the 
learned Assessing Officer had completed the assessment and passed the order under section 
144 of the Act on 07.12.2019 determining the total income of Rs. 21,49,130/- (after 
rectification) and accordingly make the addition of Rs. 26,89,881/- (after rectification) 
without considering the fact that none of the notices issued during the assessment proceeding 
had not been severed to the appellant.  
 
On receiving the computation sheet and recovery notice and on further investigation on 
Income tax portal, the appellant came to know about the assessment which was framed under 

section 144 of the Act for AY 2017-18. The appellant appointed a counsel for the said matter 
and request the learned assessing officer for obtaining a certified copy of the assessment 
order under section 144 of the Act on 26.03.2020. Copy of E-mail for obtaining certified 
copy of order is enclosed as Annexure_3.  
 
However, no reply was received. Somehow appellant managed to login into the portal by 
updating his contact details so that further actions could be taken and extracted the 
assessment order from the e-filing portal.  
 
On perusal of the order, it has been noticed that the learned assessing officer had completed 
the assessment of the appellant under section 144 of the Act vide order dated 07.12.2019. 
Copy of the assessment order is enclosed as Annexure_4. 
 
2.4 The documents mentioned in para 1.1 to 2.3 are being produced for the first time before your 
goodself. These could not be produced earlier as the Learned Assessing Officer completed 
the assessment under section 144 of the Act and no documents could be filed before him due 
to non-receipt of any notice by the appellant. Therefore, it is requested that the aforesaid 
documents may please be accepted as additional evidence under Rule 46A of the income Tax 
Rules, 1962. 
 
2.5 In this regard, it is imperative to analyse the provisions of section 144 of the Act. Relevant 
extract of the said section is as under: 
 
 If any person: 
 
(a) fails to make the return required under sub-section (1) of section 139 and has not 
made a return or a revised return under sub-section (4) or sub-section (5) of that 
section, or  
(b) fails to comply with all the terms of a notice issued under sub-section (1) of section 
142 or fails to comply with a direction issued under sub-section (2A) of that section, 
or  
(c) having made a return, fails to comply with all the terms of a notice issued under 
sub-section (2) of section 143.  
 

the Assessing Officer, after taking into account all relevant material which the Assessing 
Officer has gathered, shall, after giving the assessee an opportunity of being heard make 
the assessment of the total income or loss to the best of his judgement and determined the 
sum payable by the assessee on the basis of such assessment: 
 
Provided that such opportunity shall be given by the Assessing Officer by serving a 
notice calling upon the assessee to show cause, on a date and time to be specified in the 
notice, why the assessment should not be completed to the best of his judgement;  
 
Provided further that it shall not be necessary to give such opportunity in a case where a 
notice under sub-section (1) of section 142 has been issued prior to the making of an 
assessment under this section. 
 
2.6 In view of the said section, it is submitted that for invoking the provisions section 144 of the 
Act, there has to be a failure on the part of the assessee to comply with the notice issued 
under section 142(1) or section 143(2) of the Act. This necessary implies that the assessee 
must have received the notice and only then would the question of non-compliance of 
the notice arise. 
 
In the present case, as explained above, the appellant did not receive any notice for hearing 
under section 142(1) of the Act, neither is there any proof from the tax authorities that the 
notices were duly served on the appellant. Therefore, invoking of provisions under section 
144 of the Act is not valid.  
 
2.7 It is also pertinent to mention here that the income tax department was aware of the 
address of the appellant, however, did not send any notice to the appellant on his 
address. If a computation of statement and notice of demand can be sent on address, 
then it is difficult to comprehend as to why no notice was sent on address in respect of 
the assessment proceedings for the year under consideration. 
 
Merely because a notice is not returned unserved, does not lead to the inference that the 
notice has been served. Reliance in this regard can be placed on the decision of Hon’ble 
Allahabad High Court in the case of Suresh Kumar Sheetlani v. ITO [2018] 96 
taxmann.com 401. In this case, the department was fully aware of the correct address of the 

assessee, however, notice was sent at an incorrect address available with the bank of the 
assessee. It was held that when department had the correct address of assessee, sending notice 
at incorrect address available with bank and then drawing presumption of service of notice on 
ground that notice was not received back unserved, cannot be sustained. 
 
Further, where a best judgment assessment has been made under section 144 of the Act 
because of default in complying with any of the notices referred to in that section, and the 
assessee contends that no such notice was received by him, the onus is on the department to 
prove that such a notice was properly served on the assessee. In the absence of such proof, the 
assessment so framed, is not valid. There is no such proof by the tax authorities that the 
notices were served on the appellant. 
 
As per the assessment order, the contention of the learned Assessing Officer that the notice 
under section 142(1) was served to the appellant through ITBA, Speed Post No. 
ED042632034IN, which is also remained uncompiled with is not correct. In this regard, it is 
respectfully submitted that the notice was not received by the appellant, a copy of a 
screenshot containing the given consignment number is attached in Annexure_2. The 
consignment number provided by the Learned Assessing Officer is not traceable as proved in 
Annexure_2. 
 
2.8 Reliance in this regard can be placed on the following judicial pronouncements: 
 
(i) CIT vs Dr. K.C. Verma [2004] 266 ITR 476 (Delhi High Court) 
In this case it was held that where the revenue failed to produce any evidence to show 
that any notice under section 142(1) was served on assessee before framing 
assessment under section 144, assessment order passed under section 144 was 
unsustainable. 
 
(ii) Kush Leasing (P.) Ltd. V. ITO [2008] 20 SOT 337 (Delhi ITAT) 
In this case, it was held that where the Assessing Officer had framed the assessment 
of the assessee under section 144 of the Act without serving on it notice as envisaged 
in first proviso to section 144(1) of the Act, the Assessing Officer had erred in 
making assessment under section 144 of the Act and therefore, the said assessment 
order was held to be bad in law. 

 
(iii) Banwarilal Bhartiya v. ITO [2004] 4 SOT 311 (JODH.) (SMC) 
In this case it was held that assessment made under section 144 without 
proper service of notices under sections 142(1) and 143(2) is in violation of 
principles of natural justice and cannot be said to be valid assessment and therefore, 
was to be declared as bad in law and liable to be quashed. 
 
Copies of above judicial pronouncements are enclosed as Annexure_5. 
 
2.9 Without prejudice to the above, it is submitted that since this was the first year of e-
proceeding. Being a normal assessee who only uses his e-filing portal at the time of filing the 
income tax return and as stated above that no communication had been made with him about 
the proceeding initiation. The appellant had only received the computation sheet and recovery 
notice in the month of February 2020, so that is the reason why the appellant had not aware of 
the fact that learned assessing officer had initiated any proceeding on him and failed to comply 
with the notices. 
2.10 In view of the above legal and factual submissions, it is respectfully submitted that the 
proceedings under section 144 of the Act are bad in law and void-ab-initio and hence, the 
assessment should be quashed. 
 
 
Ground No.3 
Without prejudice to ground 2 above, the learned Assessing Officer 
has erred in making an addition of Rs. 21,49,429/- to the total income 
of the appellant on account of unexplained money held by the 
appellant under section 69A of the Act without giving credence to 
the fact that the appellant was regularly declaring the income and 
paying tax under presumptive scheme provided u/s 44AD of the 
Income Tax Act. 
 
3.1 The appellant is an Individual, filing his return of Income under section 44AD of the Act, 
During the relevant assessment year, the learned Assessing Officer found that the appellant 
had deposited cash of Rs. 21,49,429/- (cash of Rs. 18,80,501 + other credit of Rs. 2,68,628) in 
his bank accounts which stands unexplained.  

3.2 Therefore, the learned assessing officer had made the addition under section 69A of the Act 
amounting to Rs. 21,49,429/- and accordingly raised the demand Rs. 26,89,881/-. 
 
3.3 In this regard, it is essential that the provisions of section 69A of the Act be extracted 
hereunder: - 
Where in any financial year the assessee is found to be the owner of any money, bullion, 
jewellery or other valuable article and such money, bullion, jewellery or valuable article is 
not recorded in the books of account, if any, maintained by him for any source of income, and 
the assessee offers no explanation about the nature and source of acquisition of the money, 
bullion, jewellery or other valuable article, or the explanation offered by him is not, in the 
opinion of the Assessing Officer, satisfactory, the money and the value of the bullion, jewellery 
or other valuable article may be deemed to be the income of the assessee for such financial 
year. 
On a reading of section 69A , it is clear that Section 69A of the Act, can be invoked only when 
the assesse has not recorded such money in the books of accounts and offers no explanation or 
unsatisfactory explanation.  Hence, both the conditions are cumulative and satisfaction of 
either of condition does not automatically triggers rigours of section 69A. 
Means, we can say that when the assessee has recorded such money in his books of accounts 
then no explanation is required to be offered for the purpose of section 69A.  Therefore, 
Addition u/s 69A can be made only when such money is not recoded in the books of accounts 
and not offered satisfactory reply. 
3.4 In this regard, it is pertinent to refer to the provisions of Section 44AD of the Act, the relevant 
extract of which are as under: 
 
“Notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in sections 28 to 43C, in the case of an 
eligible assessee engaged in an eligible business, a sum equal to eight per cent. of the total 
turnover or gross receipts of the assessee in the previous year on account of such business or, 
as the case may be, a sum higher than the aforesaid sum claimed to have been earned by the 
eligible assessee, shall be deemed to be the profits and gains of such business chargeable to tax 
under the head "Profits and gains of business or profession". 
The provisions of this section, notwithstanding anything contained in the foregoing 
provisions, shall not apply to- 

(i)  a person carrying on profession as referred to in sub-section (1) of section 44AA; 
(ii)  a person earning income in the nature of commission or brokerage; or 
(iii) a person carrying on any agency business. 
3.5 Further, the provisions of section 44AA of the Act be extracted hereunder: - 
(1) Every person carrying on legal, medical, engineering or architectural profession or the 
profession of accountancy or technical consultancy or interior decoration or any other 
profession as is notified by the Board in the Official Gazette shall keep and maintain such 
books of account and other documents as may enable the Assessing Officer to compute his 
total income in accordance with the provisions of this Act. 
3.6 In the view of section 44AD, if person filing income tax return under section 44AD then he is 
not requiring to maintain books of accounts as per section 44AD. In the present case, appellant 
is an individual who’s for the previous years, has been disclosing the income under the 
provisions of section 44AD on presumptive basis. The appellant has shown the profits above 
the normal limits of the provisions of section 44AD. The appellant has shown 13.91% and 
12.66% profit of its sales for the Assessment Years 2015-16 and 2016-17 respectively.  Hence, 
he does not require to maintain book of accounts. Therefore, the addition made by the learned 
assessing officer under section 69A of the Act is not in accordance with provision of Income 
Tax Act. 
3.7 Further, it is clear that the onus is upon the learned Assessing Officer to find the assessee to be 
the owner of any money, bullion, jewellery or valuable article and such money, bullion, 
jewellery or valuable article was not recorded in the books of account, if any, maintained by 
the assessee for any source of income. 
3.8 In light of the provisions discussed above, the appellant is an individual who is an eligible 
assessee engaged in an eligible business. He is engaged in the business of trading in grocery 
items. The appellant had been filing his Income Tax Return for the Assessment Years 2015-16 
and 206-17 under section 44AD on presumptive basis and as a responsible taxpayer he showed 
Net Profits as 13.91% and 12.66% for both the Assessment Years respectively. Considering 
that the Net Profits shown were more than 8% of the sales for both the Assessment Years 
2015-16 and 2016-17, the learned assessing officer has erred both in law and on facts in 
completing the assessment by considering 100% of cash deposits as unexplained income and 
taxed the entire amount under section 115BBE. Annexure_4 can be referred for the same. 
 

Assessee opting to file return u/s 44AD is not obliged to explain individual entry of cash 
deposit in bank unless the AO proves that the said cash deposit has no nexus with gross receipts 
and also 44AD does not ask to maintain the books of accounts in order to support the 
expenditure of 92% of the gross receipts. 
 
The appellant wants to oppose the impugned order by the learned Assessing Officer and wants 
his income for the Assessment year 2017-18 to be taxed under Section 44AD on presumptive 
basis. Hence the additions so made and the tax liability so computed are otherwise too 
unjustified and not sustainable. Also, the learned assessing officer passed the order under 
section 144 on the basis of suspicion and doubt and also ignoring that the appellant had been 
paying taxes under Section 44AD for the preceding Assessment Years. 
 
Considering the above submission, the order passed by the learned assessing officer is void and 
accordingly, a direction may please be given to the Assessing Officer to kindly rectify the 
computation and assess the tax liability under section 44AD. 
 
3.9 Further, In appellant case, the learned Assessing Officer can resort to making an addition 
under section 69A of the Act only in respect of such monies / assets / articles or things which 
are not recorded in the assessee's books of account. However, in the present case, the appellant 
is not maintaining books of accounts as he is paying taxes under section 44AD. So, as per 
section 69A the onus is on the learned Assessing Officer to provide a chance to the appellant 
to offer an explanation about the nature and source of acquisition of the money. With this 
regard the appellant was offered no opportunity to offer explanation about the nature and

7. We have considered the rival stands carefully. The first issue in this appeal relates to the validity of
assumption of jurisdiction by the Assessing Officer by issuance of notice under section 148 dated 16-3-2004.
In terms of section 147 where the Assessing Officer has reasons to believe that any income chargeable to tax
has escaped assessment for any assessment year, he may subject to the provisions of sections 148 to 153
bring to tax such income. To resolve the controversy in this appeal the presence of expression ‘reasons to
believe’ in section 147 is relevant. The expression ‘reasons to believe’ as appearing in section 147 has been
the subject-matter of consideration by various Courts. A reference can be made to the judgments of the
Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of ITO v. Lakhmani Mewal Das [1976] 103 ITR 437 as also the decision in
the case of Ganga Saran & Sons (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [1981] 130 ITR 1. On the basis of the aforesaid judgments, it
is safe to deduce that the reasons which enable an Assessing Officer to form a belief that certain income had
escaped assessment must have a rational connection with or relevant bearing on the formation of belief. In
other words the expression ‘reasons to believe’ postulates that there must be a nexus or live link between the
material coming to the notice of the Assessing Officer and the formation of his belief that there has been an
escapement of income of the assessee from assessment in the particular assessment year. Moreover, the
Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of S. Narayanappa v. CIT [1967] 63 ITR 219 held that the expression
‘reason to believe’ does not mean a purely subjective assessment on the part of the Assessing Officer and
that the reason must be held in good faith and it cannot be merely a pretence. Furthermore, it is also a trite
law that the Courts cannot enquire into the sufficiency of reasons in the formation of requisite belief. The
jurisdiction in this regard merely extends to examining as to whether the reasons recorded have a rational
connection or relevance to the formation of belief that certain income belonging to the assessee had escaped
